subject: Agriculture
title: IR8 and the Rice Miracle
description: A quick, practical guide to IR8 and the Rice Miracle.

hook.text: In 1966, IRRI in the Philippines released IR8—a rice variety that yielded twice as much as traditional types.

buildup.text: IR8 was semi-dwarf, like Borlaug's wheat. Short stalks held heavy grain without falling over.

discovery.text: With fertilizer, IR8 could produce 10 tons per hectare—unheard of for rice at the time.

twist.text: IR8 didn't taste great. Farmers grew it for yield but ate traditional varieties when they could afford to.

climax.text: Later varieties like IR36 and IR64 combined high yield with better taste and disease resistance.

punchline.text: IR8 fed millions. Its successors fed billions.

quiz.question: What was special about the IR8 rice variety?
options: It was semi-dwarf and yielded twice as much as traditional rice

details.summary: IR8, nicknamed 'miracle rice,' was the first high-yielding semi-dwarf rice variety developed by the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) in 1966. It doubled rice yields across tropical Asia and is credited with preventing famine for millions across the Philippines, India, and Indonesia.
details.whyItMatters: Rice feeds more people than any other crop. IR8 proved that the same dwarfing revolution that transformed wheat could work for rice, extending the Green Revolution's benefits to the billions who depend on rice as their staple food.
takeaways: IR8 was developed at IRRI in the Philippines by crossing Indonesian and Chinese varieties
It yielded 5-10 tons per hectare compared to 1-2 tons for traditional varieties
IR8 was adopted across tropical Asia within years, dramatically reducing rice shortages

faq.question: Why was IR8 called miracle rice?
faq.answer: IR8 produced 5-10 tons per hectare—up to 10 times more than traditional tall rice varieties with proper inputs. It was short-stemmed, fertilizer-responsive, and matured in 130 days instead of 180, allowing double cropping. Its dramatic yield increases seemed miraculous to farmers facing hunger.

faq.question: What were the limitations of IR8 and early Green Revolution rice?
faq.answer: IR8 had poor cooking quality and taste compared to traditional varieties. It required expensive fertilizer and irrigation to achieve its potential. It was susceptible to several pests and diseases. Later IRRI varieties (IR36, IR64) addressed these problems while maintaining high yields.
